unit.unitOverview: Communication is transferring information from one person to another, by speaking or writing, in a way that the other person truly understands. It is not just talking. Real communication means knowing your purpose and audience, organising a clear message with reasoning and evidence, presenting it well by voice or visual, and listening carefully to others.

explainers.title: Welcome to your final Year 8 unit
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome to Unit 6 of Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. This is the last unit of Year 8, and it teaches the sixth and final Global Perspectives skill: Communication. You have travelled a long way over two years of this subject, and this is the unit where all of that work finally reaches other people.

Remember the six skills you have been growing:

Communication comes last for a good reason: it is the skill that brings all the others together. You can research an issue thoroughly, analyse it deeply, evaluate it fairly and reflect on it honestly, but if you cannot share what you have learned, it stays locked inside your own head. Communication is how your thinking becomes something a listener can hear, a reader can follow, and a whole community can act on.

In Stage 8 you go further than you did last year. You will not just speak clearly; you will plan and deliver a persuasive, well-structured piece for a specific audience and purpose, build each paragraph as a small argument, weave in evidence from your own research, choose your register with care, and reflect on how your audience actually responded. This is what skilled communicators do in the real world.
bullets: Research — finding things out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — taking a topic apart to see its causes, effects and connections.
Evaluation — judging how strong an argument or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking honestly about how you learn and how your views change.
Collaboration — working well with other people towards a shared goal.
Communication — sharing your ideas so clearly that others truly understand.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning the Ehel Academy way, which is self-paced. Three kinds of support work together, and in Stage 8 you take a little more of the lead yourself:

Older versions of this subject told learners to 'present to the class' or 'share with your group'. In our model, your presentation has two stages. First you rehearse with your AI tutor, who acts as a fair, honest audience and helps you improve as many times as you need. Then you deliver the real thing in your teacher session, and often to your family and community as well. So every 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box is a rehearsal in front of a real listener. Say your ideas out loud, and let the tutor tell you what came across clearly and what did not.
bullets: You, learning at your own pace. You read, think and complete each activity in your own time. Slow down to rehearse a tricky sentence; move quickly through an idea you already know.

Your AI tutor, available every hour of the day. Whenever this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor as if it were both a patient practice audience and an honest coach. It listens to your ideas, questions your thinking, and gives feedback whenever you are ready, day or night.
Your teacher, about twice a week. Your live sessions are where you deliver your real presentation, hear other learners, give and receive feedback, and get guidance on where to go next.

explainers.title: Meet Imani, our communicator for this unit
explainers.body:
To make every skill concrete, we will follow one Year 8 learner all the way through this unit. Her name is Imani, and she studies at Ehel Academy in Berbera, on the coast.

All year, Imani has been working on one Challenge: the plastic waste along Berbera's coast and streets. She noticed thin plastic bags snagged in the market, blown into drains, and washed up on the beach where fishers land their boats. Over the year she researched the problem with a survey of families and shoppers and by observing the beach and market, analysed what causes the waste and what it leads to, evaluated several possible solutions to see which would help most, and reflected on how her own view changed as she learned more.

Now Imani reaches the final step. She has strong findings and a fair, well-judged opinion, but they are still sitting in her notebook. In this unit she must communicate them: turn a year of thinking into a clear, convincing piece that her teacher, her family and the wider community of Berbera could understand and act on. As you meet each new skill, you will see exactly what Imani does with it, and you will be doing the very same thing with your own Challenge.

explainers.title: Your Challenge comes together and is shared
explainers.body:
All year your work has been building towards one ongoing project we call your Challenge: a global issue that also matters right where you live. In each unit you added another skill to it. Communication is the unit where the Challenge finally comes together and is shared with an audience.

Think of your Challenge as a house you have been building all year. Research laid the foundations. Analysis and Evaluation raised the walls and checked they were strong. Reflection made sure they were straight. Communication is the moment you open the door and invite people inside. Everything you present in this unit rests on the work you have already done.

explainers.title: What is communication, really?
explainers.body:
Many people think communication just means talking. In Global Perspectives it means something more careful. Communication is transferring information from one person to another, by speaking or writing, in a way that the other person truly understands. The test of good communication is not whether you spoke, but whether your listener understood.

Communication has two halves that matter equally. These are exactly the two things the Cambridge objectives ask of you:

Weak communicators only think about the first half. Strong communicators do both: they make themselves clear, and they listen closely to others. You will practise both halves in this unit, because in Stage 8 a good communicator is judged on speaking and listening together.
bullets: Expressing — presenting your own information and arguments clearly, with reasoning, and referencing your sources. This is objective 8Mi.01.
Listening — taking in other people's ideas carefully and offering relevant, well-judged contributions that show you understood the issue. This is objective 8Ml.01.

explainers.title: Skill 1: Knowing your purpose and audience
explainers.body:
Before you plan a single sentence, a strong communicator asks two questions: What is my purpose? and Who is my audience? These two answers shape everything else you do.

The same message must be shaped differently for different audiences. Explaining plastic waste to a class of six-year-olds needs simple words and a friendly voice. Writing to the town council needs a more formal tone and your strongest evidence first. Same topic, different shape, because the audience is different.
bullets: Purpose is why you are communicating. Do you want to inform people, persuade them, or raise awareness? Your purpose decides what you include.
Audience is who you are communicating with. Their age, their knowledge and their interests decide how you say it.

explainers.title: Skill 2: Finding your key message
explainers.body:
Every good piece of communication has one key message: the single most important idea you want your audience to remember. If your listener forgot everything else but remembered your key message, you would still have succeeded. Weak communication has no clear message, so the audience is left wondering what the point was.

You need this skill in two directions. When you read or listen, you should be able to find someone else's key message. When you create, you should be able to say your own key message in one clear sentence. A useful Stage 8 habit is to keep that sentence short: short sentences are easier for an audience to hold in mind and repeat later.

explainers.title: Skill 3: Structuring your piece - introduction, body and conclusion
explainers.body:
A clear message needs a clear structure. Text structure is simply how a piece is organised so the audience can follow it easily. Almost every strong talk, essay or article is built from three parts:

In Stage 8 two things matter more than before. First, your conclusion should not only summarise; it should share your own reasoned view of the issue, reached after weighing causes, consequences and different perspectives. Second, you should start a new paragraph deliberately: when you begin a new point, when you compare information, and when you move from your introduction into the body or from the body into your conclusion.
bullets: Introduction — links to your title or research question, and makes clear what the piece is about and what you believe.
Body — the middle, made of several paragraphs, where each paragraph carries one main point with its reasoning and evidence.
Conclusion — draws your points together, sums up the evidence, and gives your personal perspective, without adding any new idea.

explainers.title: Skill 4: Building each paragraph as a structured argument
explainers.body:
Often your purpose is to persuade, and that means building an argument. In Global Perspectives, an argument is not a quarrel; it is a claim backed up by good thinking. At Stage 8, each body paragraph should itself be a small, complete argument with three parts:

This is exactly where your earlier skills pay off. Your evidence comes from your Research. Your reasoning often comes from your Analysis of causes and effects. Your judgement about which solution is best comes from your Evaluation. Communication does not invent new material; it arranges the material you already earned into a convincing shape, one paragraph at a time.
bullets: A claim — the point you want your audience to accept, such as 'thin plastic bags harm our town'.
Reasoning — why the claim is true, such as 'because they block drains and reach the sea'.
Evidence — the fact, number or example that supports the reasoning, such as a survey result or an observation.

explainers.title: Skill 5: Reasoning and transition words
explainers.body:
Good communication does not just list facts; it connects them so the audience can follow your thinking. You do this with transition words, sometimes called linking words. They act like signposts that tell your audience what is coming next.

Three kinds are especially useful in an argument:

Used well, transition words turn a pile of separate facts into a smooth, reasoned argument. Reach for them especially at the joins: when you move from a claim to its reasoning, when you introduce evidence, and when you begin your conclusion.
bullets: Words that give reasoning — such as 'because', 'so that', 'therefore', 'this means that' and 'as a result'. They show why something matters.
Words that introduce evidence — such as 'for example', 'for instance', 'such as' and 'to demonstrate'. They tell the audience a fact is coming.
Words that conclude — such as 'finally', 'in conclusion', 'to sum up' and 'as you can see'. They signal that you are drawing everything together.

explainers.title: Skill 6: Writing a script and presenting out loud
explainers.body:
At Stage 8 you often write a script first: your whole argument set down in order, ready to be read aloud, recorded, or turned into notes. Writing the script forces your structure to be clear. Then, when you present, how you speak matters almost as much as what you say. Clear speaking is a set of habits anyone can learn, not a magic gift.

The single best way to improve is to rehearse out loud before the real thing. You can also record your argument as a short podcast or voice note and listen back, which quickly shows you where you rushed or lost the thread. This is where your AI tutor is perfect: you can present to it again and again, at any hour, and it will tell you honestly whether you were clear.
bullets: Speak slowly and clearly. Nervous speakers rush. Slow down, and give your audience time to take each idea in.
Give detail, but stay on your point. Enough detail to be convincing, not so much that your message is buried.
Use notes, not the full script. A few bullet points on a card keep you on track without you reading every word.
Look up. Making eye contact, even now and then, shows the audience you are talking to them.

explainers.title: Skill 7: Presenting visually and creatively
explainers.body:
Not all communication is a straight talk. Often a visual or a creative outcome carries your message faster than plain words. A good visual is not decoration; it helps the audience understand something more quickly, or feel why it matters.

Useful tools in Global Perspectives include:
bullets: Simple charts — a bar chart or table shows a number pattern in a second, far faster than a sentence. If your evidence is numbers, a chart is often the clearest choice.
Posters and slogans — a short, memorable phrase raises awareness because people remember it.
Creative outcomes — a rap, a song, a poem or a short video can raise awareness in a way that sticks in the mind and reaches people a formal report never would.

explainers.title: Skill 8: Choosing suitable language and register
explainers.body:
Register means the level of formality in your language, and choosing the right level for your audience. You already do this without thinking: you speak to a young child differently from the way you speak to a head teacher. Matching your register to your audience is a real Stage 8 communication skill.

Clear communication also means using the right topic-specific words and spelling them correctly, because precise words help an audience trust you and follow you. Getting register wrong sends the wrong signal: language too casual for the council may seem as if you are not taking the issue seriously, while language too formal for young children will simply lose them. Picture your audience and ask: what language would they take seriously and understand?
bullets: Formal register — careful, polite, no slang. Suits a letter to officials, or a serious presentation.
Friendly register — warm and simple, still respectful. Suits younger audiences, family, or awareness posters.

explainers.title: Skill 9: Listening actively and recording others' ideas
explainers.body:
Communication is a two-way street, so listening is half the skill, and objective 6.2 is all about it. Active listening means attentively trying to understand what someone means, rather than just hearing their words while you wait for your turn to speak. It is one of the most respectful things you can do for another person, and it is very different from passive hearing.

You show active listening with feedback of two kinds:

Active listening also lets you record other people's ideas accurately, which you will need when you gather views for your Challenge or listen to another learner's argument in your teacher session. Listen for the person's key message and their evidence, then note it down in your own words so you could repeat it back fairly.
bullets: Non-verbal feedback — showing you are listening without words: nodding, leaning forward, and making eye contact.
Verbal feedback — short spoken signals such as 'I see', 'I understand' and 'that makes sense'.

explainers.title: Skill 10: Giving and receiving feedback to improve
explainers.body:
In Stage 8, communication is not a single try; it is a loop. You share a draft, you get feedback, and you use it to improve. So you must learn to give feedback well and to receive it well. Good feedback follows three fair rules:

Receiving feedback is a skill too. Listen without defending yourself, thank the person, and pick the one or two changes that would help most. Then actually improve your work and rehearse it again. A communicator who welcomes feedback improves far faster than one who takes it as an attack.
bullets: Start with the positive, and give more positives than negatives.
Talk about the work, not the person. 'Your evidence in point two was convincing' helps; 'you are a bad speaker' only hurts.
Be specific and give an example, so the other person knows exactly what to change.

explainers.title: Skill 11: Communicating fairly and checking your facts
explainers.body:
Global Perspectives is about seeing an issue from many sides. So when you communicate, represent different perspectives fairly, not just your own. An audience trusts a communicator who has clearly listened to more than one point of view and who gives credit for the evidence they use.

Three habits make your communication fair and trustworthy:

Remember too that the type of source shapes the kind of information you get: a personal blog usually gives an opinion, while a scientific report usually gives checked facts. Naming your sources and cross-checking them is how you make sure your persuasive piece is also a truthful one.
bullets: Represent other perspectives. Mention the views of people who see the issue differently, and treat them fairly, even as you argue your own case and give your personal perspective.
Reference your sources. When your evidence comes from a book, website, report or person, say so. This is honest, it avoids copying, and it lets your audience check your facts.
Cross-check your facts. Before you rely on a fact, confirm it appears on more than one trustworthy source. This is called cross-referencing, and it protects you from repeating something false.

explainers.title: Skill 12: Reflecting on how your audience responded
explainers.body:
The last part of communication happens after you present. A thoughtful communicator watches and listens to how the audience responded, then uses what they notice to improve next time. This is where Communication joins hands with Reflection, the skill you built earlier in the year.

After you present, ask yourself:

Audience reactions are information, not judgement. A confused look is not a failure; it is a clue that points you to the sentence you need to fix. A good question is not a criticism; it shows you where your piece had a gap. Every presentation you give makes the next one stronger, as long as you reflect on it honestly.
bullets: Did my audience understand my key message? How could I tell?
Which part landed well, and which part left them confused or bored?
What questions did they ask, and what do those questions tell me was unclear?
What impact did my piece have — did anyone say they would do something differently?

explainers.title: How Communication draws on all five earlier skills
explainers.body:
Communication comes last because it needs the other five. A strong presentation is really the other skills, made visible to an audience. Look at how each one feeds in:

So when you communicate your Challenge, you are not starting from nothing. You are gathering everything you built all year and presenting it as one clear, fair, convincing whole. That is why this skill comes last: it is the destination the other five were leading to.
bullets: Research gives you the facts and sources that become your evidence. Without research, you would have nothing true to say.
Analysis gives you the reasoning: the causes and effects you found when you broke the topic apart.
Evaluation gives you your judgement: which solution is strongest, and why your audience should accept it.
Reflection gives you your personal perspective and helps you improve, as you notice how your audience responded.
Collaboration gives you the habits of listening and feedback, so presenting and discussing with others goes well.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: Imani's Challenge, communicated
explainers.body: You have now met every communication skill in this unit. Here is how Imani used them to turn a year of work into one clear piece.

explainers.title: You have completed the Year 8 skills journey
explainers.body:
Take a moment to see how far you have come. Across this year you met Research and learned to find things out carefully and fairly. Then Analysis taught you to break an issue apart, Evaluation taught you to judge how strong ideas really are, Reflection taught you to learn from your own thinking, and Collaboration taught you to work well with others. Now Communication has taught you to share it all clearly, fairly and convincingly with the world.

These six skills are not just for Global Perspectives. They are for the rest of your life: for the choices you will make, the problems you will help solve, and the ideas you will one day need to explain to others. A person who can research, analyse, evaluate, reflect, collaborate and communicate can take on almost anything.

Well done for reaching the end of Year 8 and the end of your Lower Secondary Global Perspectives journey. Finish this unit by communicating your Challenge as clearly and fairly as you can, be proud of the thinker you have become, and carry these six skills forward. In the Activities file, your final presentation is waiting.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to hold on to
lines: Communication is not just talking. It is making sure another person truly understands you.
It works in two directions: getting your own message across clearly, and listening carefully to others.
In this unit, everything you researched, analysed and evaluated across Year 8 turns into one clear, convincing piece you can present.

bigIdeas.title: Who is your audience in this unit?
lines: Your AI tutor is your rehearsal audience. Practise with it as often as you like, at any hour, until your message is clear.
Your teacher session, about twice a week, is where you deliver the real presentation and give and receive feedback with your teacher and other learners.
Your family and community are a real audience too. Sharing your Challenge at home, or as a poster in your neighbourhood, is one of the most powerful things you can do.

You do not have to make it perfect on the first try. Communication improves with rehearsal, exactly like a sport or a song. That is why your AI tutor matters so much: it will listen and give feedback as many times as you need, without ever getting tired.

bigIdeas.title: A trick for finding a key message
lines: Look for words or ideas that are repeated. Writers and speakers repeat what matters most.
Ask: what is the one thing this person most wants me to remember?
Try to say it in a single short sentence. If you cannot, keep trimming until you can.

bigIdeas.title: Claim, reasoning, evidence - the backbone of a paragraph
lines: Claim: the point you are making in this paragraph.
Reasoning: why that point is true, often signalled by the word because.
Evidence: the fact, number or example that proves the reasoning.
A claim with no evidence is only an opinion. Evidence is what makes an audience believe you.

bigIdeas.title: What makes a strong slogan or line
lines: Keep it short. Short sentences and lines are easy to remember.
Make the point clear at a glance, with no confusing words.
Where you can, give a reason or a feeling, so it sticks in the mind.
Example shape: a strong phrase, then a reason — Clean coast, full nets.

bigIdeas.title: Fair feedback against clear criteria
lines: Agree what a strong piece needs: a clear message, structure, evidence, reasoning, references and a fitting register.
Give feedback against those criteria, not against the person.
Start positive, be specific, and offer one clear idea to improve.

bigIdeas.title: A fairness note for Global Perspectives
lines: A fair communicator can present an issue that different families feel differently about — such as whether the school calendar should mark holidays for both Eid and Christmas — by giving each viewpoint honestly and evenly.
You can still have your own opinion. Fairness means you form it after listening to all sides, and you let the audience hear those sides too.
Representing perspectives evenly, without putting any group down, is at the heart of good communication.

bigIdeas.title: Where this unit is heading
lines: By the end of these activities you will have a finished, well-structured piece about your Challenge.
You will rehearse it fully with your AI tutor, then deliver it in your teacher session and, if you can, to your family and community.
You will also design a visual or creative outcome, such as a poster with a slogan, to share your message quickly.

bigIdeas.title: A quick structure check
lines: Introduction: does it make clear what I am talking about and what I believe?
Body: does each point carry just one main idea?
Conclusion: does it sum up and give my personal view, with nothing new sneaking in?

bigIdeas.title: Handy transition words
lines: To give reasoning: because, so that, therefore, this means that, as a result.
To introduce evidence: for example, for instance, such as, to demonstrate.
To conclude: finally, in conclusion, to sum up, as you can see.

bigIdeas.title: Rehearsal tips
lines: Speak slowly and clearly, and pause after your key message.
Use a few bullet-point notes, not the full script read word for word.
Rehearse as many times as you like — your AI tutor never gets tired.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 6 of Stage 8 Global Perspectives, the final unit of Year 8, and the skill is Communication.
Ask it: In one or two sentences, why is clear communication a useful skill even outside of school?
Then tell the tutor which part of communicating you find hardest — speaking out loud, structuring your ideas, or listening well — and ask for one tip to start with.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you now think communication means.
Ask it: Is my definition missing anything important, such as listening or being understood?
Then try Imani's test: explain your Challenge topic to your tutor in thirty seconds, and ask whether your main message came across clearly.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your Challenge topic and what you want your audience to think, feel or do by the end.
Ask it to help you name your purpose in one word: inform, persuade, or raise awareness.
Then describe your main audience, and ask the tutor how that audience should change the way you speak or write.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your AI tutor a short passage, or ask it for one, and tell it what you think the key message is.
Ask whether you found the true main idea, and how it spotted the message.
Then say your own Challenge key message in one short sentence, and ask the tutor if it is clear and focused enough.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor the topic of your piece.
Ask it to help you draft an introduction linked to your research question, three body points, and a conclusion that sums up and adds your personal perspective.
Then check together: does each body point carry just one main idea, and does the conclusion avoid any new fact?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one claim you want to make about your Challenge.
Ask it to help you add reasoning and a real piece of evidence from your own research, analysis or evaluation.
Then ask: where did this evidence come from, and how should I reference that source when I present?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your AI tutor two or three facts from your Challenge with no linking words between them.
Ask it to help you join them using words like because, therefore and for example.
Then ask the tutor which transition words would suit the start of your conclusion.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Present your introduction and first body point out loud to your AI tutor, as if it were your audience.
Ask it: Was I clear? Did I go too fast? Was my key message easy to hear?
Ask the tutor for one specific thing to improve, then present again and see if it is better.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what evidence you have and who your visual or creative outcome is for.
Ask it whether a chart, a poster, a slogan or a short poem would show your message most clearly.
Then draft a slogan or a line for your Challenge and ask the tutor if it is short, clear and memorable.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor who your main audience is for your Challenge piece.
Ask it whether a formal or a friendly register would suit them better, and why.
Then say one sentence of your piece, and ask the tutor to rewrite it in the register that fits your audience.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to read you a short opinion on a topic, then tell it the key message back in your own words to show you listened.
Ask it to explain the difference between active listening and passive hearing, with an example of each.
Then ask the tutor for two verbal and two non-verbal signals you could use to show a speaker you are listening.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Present a piece of your own work and ask your AI tutor to give feedback using the three fair rules.
Ask it to name the one change that would most improve your piece.
Make that change, present again, and ask the tutor whether it is now clearer.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your main argument, then ask it to help you name one perspective that differs from yours.
Ask how you could mention that other view fairly without weakening your own case.
Then list the sources of your evidence and ask the tutor how to reference them simply, and how to cross-check one key fact.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: After you rehearse, tell your AI tutor which part of your piece you think was clearest and which was weakest.
Ask it to predict what questions a real audience might ask, so you can prepare answers.
Then ask the tutor to help you plan one improvement for your next rehearsal or your teacher session.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your topic, your purpose and your audience.
Ask it: Does my purpose match my audience, or should I adjust one of them?
Ask the tutor how my chosen audience should change the way I speak or write.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your key message to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Is this clear and focused, or is it trying to say too much at once?
Ask the tutor to suggest one shorter or sharper way to word my key message.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor the best evidence you have gathered and where each piece came from.
Ask it: Which piece is strongest, and which is weakest?
Ask the tutor how to mention the source of each piece of evidence when I present.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your introduction, three body points and conclusion to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the structure is clear and whether any point is doing two jobs at once.
Ask the tutor if my conclusion gives a personal perspective without adding a new fact.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read one of your paragraphs to your AI tutor as a claim, reasoning and evidence.
Ask it: Does my reasoning really explain my claim, and does my evidence really prove my reasoning?
Ask the tutor to help me strengthen the weakest of my three paragraphs.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your linked-up script to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the transition words make your reasoning clearer, or whether any feel forced.
Ask the tutor whether each of my paragraphs really starts a new point.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe your visual or creative outcome and read your slogan or line to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the form shows your message clearly and whether the line is memorable.
Ask the tutor for one way to make my slogan or line shorter or stronger.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your two versions — friendly and formal — to your AI tutor.
Ask it which register best fits my real audience, and why.
Ask the tutor to check that my script keeps that register from start to finish.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Present your full piece to your AI tutor and ask for honest feedback on clarity and pace.
Ask it to predict two questions a real audience might ask, and help me prepare answers.
Ask the tutor: what is the single most important thing to improve before my teacher session?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor how your real delivery went and what questions or feedback you received.
Ask it to help me understand what those questions show about the clearest and weakest parts of my piece.
Ask the tutor to help me plan one improvement for the next time I communicate.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three checkpoint sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Based on how my audience responded, which communication skill should I keep practising?
Ask the tutor to help me set one goal for communicating in the future.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your fixed pieces and your rewritten feedback to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your rewrites are now clear, well structured and fair.
Ask the tutor to show you one more way to improve any answer you found hard.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to tell you which answer was strongest and why.
Ask the tutor to give you one more scenario like these to try.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your reflection answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you notice how your thinking and your confidence changed across the whole year.
Ask the tutor to suggest one skill to keep sharpening next, and why.

speakingPrompts.title: Imani's starting point
lines: Imani knows a great deal about plastic waste on the coast. But when she first tried to explain it to her aunt, she jumped around: a bit about fish, a bit about her survey, a bit about drains, all mixed together.
Her aunt was kind but confused, and asked: So what are you actually asking me to do?
Imani realised the problem was not her research. It was her communication. Her message was strong but unclear.
This unit is about fixing exactly that: turning good thinking into a clear message an audience can follow and act on.

speakingPrompts.title: Imani's example: purpose and audience
lines: Purpose: Imani wants to persuade people that Berbera can cut its plastic waste, and to raise awareness so families act.
Audience 1: her teacher session and family. She will use a clear spoken presentation with a warm, respectful voice.
Audience 2: the wider community. For them she plans a poster with a short slogan, because a poster is seen quickly by many people.
Notice that Imani keeps one message but changes its shape for each audience.

speakingPrompts.title: Imani's example: one clear sentence
lines: Weak: There are lots of things about plastic and the market and the beach and the fish and the drains near our town.
Strong: Small daily choices about plastic can keep Berbera's coast clean, so let us switch to reusable bags and clean our beach together.
The strong version is one clear message an audience can remember and repeat.

speakingPrompts.title: Imani's example: the shape of her piece
lines: Introduction: Plastic waste is harming Berbera's coast, and I will show how our town can begin to fix it.
Body point 1: My survey found most families use thin plastic bags every day and few reach a bin.
Body point 2: I observed bags in the drains and on the beach, which explains the flooding and the harm to sea life.
Body point 3: Of the solutions I evaluated, reusable bags plus monthly clean-ups would help the most.
Conclusion: Weighing all the evidence, I believe reusable bags and community clean-ups are the fairest first step. No new facts, just a reasoned finish.

speakingPrompts.title: Imani's example: one paragraph as an argument
lines: Claim: Thin plastic bags are harming Berbera's coast.
Reasoning: Because they are thrown away the same day, blow into drains, and wash out to sea.
Evidence: In my survey, 18 of 25 families said they use several thin bags a day, and when I observed the beach I counted bags tangled in the fishers' nets.
She also names her sources — her own survey and observation — so the audience can trust her.

speakingPrompts.title: Zara's example: adding transition words
lines: Without links: The market floods. There are plastic bags in the drains. We should use cloth bags.
With links: The market floods because plastic bags block the drains. This means that switching to cloth bags would help. For example, one nearby town cut its flooding after banning thin bags.
The second version reasons; the first only lists. The transition words do the work.

speakingPrompts.title: Imani's example: rehearsing with her AI tutor
lines: Imani read her script in her head and thought it was fine.
Then she said it out loud to her AI tutor, which noticed she spoke very fast and never paused after her key message.
On her third rehearsal she slowed down, paused after the message, and it sounded far more convincing.
By the time of her teacher session, she had practised so often that her nerves had mostly gone.

speakingPrompts.title: Imani's example: a poster and a chant
lines: For the community, Imani designs a poster with a simple bar chart from her survey: most families use several thin bags a day.
Across the top she writes a slogan: Reuse your bag, protect our beach.
For a clean-up day, she and her friends write a short chant so younger children remember to bring a bag for their litter.
The chart gives the evidence at a glance; the slogan and chant give the message in a few memorable words.

speakingPrompts.title: Imani's example: two registers, one message
lines: To six-year-olds: The beach is where the fish live, so we always take our rubbish home with us.
To the town council: Plastic waste is damaging our coast and our fishing, and I respectfully ask the council to support reusable bags and regular clean-ups.
Same concern, two registers. Each fits its audience.

speakingPrompts.title: Sami's example: listening well
lines: In the teacher session, Sami listens to Imani rehearse instead of planning what he will say next.
He nods, and when she pauses he says: So your main point is that reusable bags would help most — is that right?
Imani says yes, and feels understood, which makes the whole discussion friendlier and more useful.
Because Sami really listened, his feedback afterwards was sharp and fair.

speakingPrompts.title: Grace's example: feedback that helps
lines: Grace listens to Imani rehearse and starts positive: Your survey evidence was really convincing.
She adds one specific, work-focused idea: I lost your key message at the start — could you say it more slowly and pause after it?
Imani thanks her, changes just that, and rehearses again — and her next version is clearly better.
That is the feedback loop working: kind, specific, and acted on.

speakingPrompts.title: Imani's example: fairness and credit
lines: Imani argues for reusable bags, but she also fairly mentions the market sellers who worry that new bags will cost them more.
By naming that other perspective honestly, she sounds fair, not one-sided.
She says where her facts came from — her own survey of 25 families, and a coastal charity's report — and checked the charity's figure against a second source.
Her audience trusts her more because she is fair, open and careful with her facts.

speakingPrompts.title: Imani's example: learning from the response
lines: After her teacher session, Imani noticed two people asked the same question: who would pay for the reusable bags?
That told her that her talk had a gap: she had no evidence about cost.
Instead of feeling bad, she added a short point about cost to her poster for the community.
The audience's questions made her communication better, and her message more convincing.

speakingPrompts.title: Imani's whole journey, from notebook to audience
lines: Skills 1 and 2: She named her purpose and audiences and wrote her key message in one short sentence.
Skills 3 and 4: She shaped her piece into introduction, body and conclusion, and built each paragraph as a claim with reasoning and evidence.
Skill 5: She joined her ideas with transition words such as because and for example.
Skills 6 and 7: She wrote a script, rehearsed out loud with her AI tutor, and designed a poster with a chart, a slogan and a clean-up-day chant.
Skill 8: She matched her register to each audience, formal for the council and friendly for children.
Skills 9 and 10: She listened actively, then gave and received feedback and improved her draft.
Skills 11 and 12: She represented other perspectives fairly, referenced and cross-checked her sources, and reflected on the questions people asked.

By following these steps, Imani turned a worry about a plastic-strewn coast into a clear, fair, evidence-backed piece that her community could act on. In the Activities file, you will do exactly the same with your own Challenge, one step at a time, rehearsing with your AI tutor and delivering in your teacher session.

speakingPrompts.title: Malik's example: purpose and audience
lines: Topic: bringing solar power to our school at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa.
Purpose: to persuade, so the school tries one solar lamp in each classroom.
Audience: his teacher and the school's head teacher.
What he wants: for the school to test solar lamps and see the saving for itself.

speakingPrompts.title: A model key message
lines: Weak: There are lots of things about the coast and plastic and the market and the fish near our town.
Strong: Reusable bags and monthly clean-ups can keep Berbera's coast clean.
The strong version is one short sentence an audience can hold in their head and repeat.

speakingPrompts.title: Leila's example: gathering evidence
lines: Leila's Challenge is about traffic near her school in Mogadishu.
From her research: 15 of 20 drivers she counted did not slow down at the corner.
From her analysis: fast traffic plus a blind corner is what makes it dangerous.
From her evaluation: she judged that a painted crossing was the cheapest useful fix.
She now has a number, a cause, and a judgement — ready to shape into paragraphs.

speakingPrompts.title: A model paragraph built as an argument
lines: Claim: Our market should switch to reusable cloth bags.
Reasoning: Because thin plastic bags block the drains and reach the sea.
Evidence: In my survey, most sellers agreed the drains flood in the rains.
Source: my own survey of 20 market sellers.

speakingPrompts.title: Model slogans and lines
lines: Plastic: Reuse your bag, protect our beach.
Water: Every drop counts — do not waste water.
Road safety: Slow down outside our school — keep students safe.
Notice each one is short, clear, and gives a reason or a feeling.

speakingPrompts.title: Yasmin's example: one message, two registers
lines: Message: girls who leave school early lose chances that are hard to get back.
Friendly (for younger students): staying in school opens doors that are hard to open later.
Formal (for a community meeting): early school-leaving among girls reduces their future opportunities, and I ask you to consider how we might support them to stay.
Same message, matched to each audience.

speakingPrompts.title: Share it at home and in your community
lines: Present your Challenge to a family member or neighbour, in a register that suits them.
Ask them what they think should be done about your topic, and listen to their answer.
Bring their response, and any questions they asked, to your next teacher session.

toolkit.title: The communication cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro:
Whatever your message, good communication follows the same steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel unsure.

The steps run in order, but you can always loop back. If a rehearsal shows your message is unclear, return to the key-message step and sharpen it. If a paragraph has no evidence, return to your Year 8 research. Good communicators move around this cycle more than once before they present.
items: Purpose and audience: decide why you are communicating and who for.
Key message: say your one main idea in a single short sentence.
Structure: organise it into an introduction, a body and a conclusion.
Argument: build each paragraph as a claim, reasoning and evidence, and name your sources.
Rehearse: practise out loud with your AI tutor and improve.
Deliver: present in your teacher session, and to family and community.
Feedback and reflect: give and receive feedback, notice how your audience responded, and improve.

toolkit.title: The Communication skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Communication is transferring information from one person to another, by speaking or writing, in a way that the other person truly understands. It is not just talking. Real communication means knowing your purpose and audience, organising a clear message with reasoning and evidence, presenting it well by voice or visual, and listening carefully to others.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, always think about your audience, because a message only works if the person in front of you understands it. Second, remember communication is two-way: you must listen and give feedback as carefully as you speak. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: Cambridge Stage 8 Communication objectives
toolkit.intro:
Global Perspectives sets out exactly what strong communication looks like at this stage. There are two Communication objectives, restated simply below. Your teacher may refer to these codes.

Notice that these two objectives cover the two halves of communication. Objective 6.1 is about expressing your own ideas well: clearly, with reasoning, and with sources named. Objective 6.2 is about listening well: taking in what others say and responding in a way that shows you understood. A strong communicator grows both together, not just the speaking half.

rows: Present information and arguments clearly with some reasoning, referencing sources where appropriate.
Share your ideas and arguments clearly, give reasons, and say where your evidence came from.
Listen to ideas and information and offer relevant and well-judged contributions that demonstrate understanding of the issue.
Listen carefully to others, then add helpful, sensible comments that show you understood the issue.

toolkit.title: Planner: Audience and purpose
toolkit.intro:
Fill this in before you plan anything. Copy the table into your notebook and answer each question.

The most common mistake is to skip this planner and jump straight to writing. Five minutes spent answering these questions will save you an hour of confusion later, because every other choice you make depends on knowing your audience and your purpose.

rows: Who is my audience?
What do they already know about my topic?
What is my purpose: inform, persuade, or raise awareness?
What is my one key message?
Which form fits best: a talk, a poster, a chart, a slogan, a poem?
What language and register will suit this audience?

toolkit.title: Template: Introduction, body and conclusion
toolkit.intro:
Use this outline to shape any presentation or piece of writing. Each body paragraph should carry one point, its reasoning and its evidence.

Three body paragraphs is a good number for a Stage 8 piece: enough to be convincing, not so many that your audience loses track. If you have more, choose your three strongest and let the rest go. Start a new paragraph for each new point.

rows: Introduction
Link to your title or research question, say what the piece is about, and state your key message.
Body paragraph 1
First point, with reasoning and evidence (and its source).
Body paragraph 2
Second point, with reasoning and evidence (and its source).
Body paragraph 3
Third point, with reasoning and evidence (and its source).
Conclusion
Sum up your points and give your personal perspective. Add nothing new.

toolkit.title: Template: Building a paragraph as an argument
toolkit.intro:
Turn any point into a convincing paragraph by filling in these four rows.

Repeat this pattern for each of your body paragraphs. Three short paragraphs, each with a claim, reasoning and evidence, make a far more convincing piece than a long list of facts with no shape.

rows: Claim
The point I want my audience to accept.
Reasoning
Why the claim is true (often starts with 'because').
Evidence
The fact, number or example that proves the reasoning.
Source
Where the evidence came from (and, ideally, a second source that agrees).

toolkit.title: Referencing and checking your sources
toolkit.intro:
Objective 6.1 asks you to reference sources 'where appropriate'. You do not need a full written reference list for a short spoken talk, but you should still say where your evidence came from, in a natural sentence. Before you rely on an important fact, cross-check it: confirm it appears on more than one trustworthy source.

Simple ways to reference out loud:

Remember that the type of source shapes the information: a personal blog usually gives an opinion, while a scientific report usually gives checked facts. If your piece is written rather than spoken, add a short reference list at the end, giving the author, title, date and where you found each source.
items: In my own survey of ... people, I found that ...
According to a report by ... , ...
As one fisher I interviewed told me, ...
A leaflet from ... (name the organisation) says that ...

toolkit.title: Giving and receiving feedback
toolkit.intro: Feedback is how a piece gets better. Use these frames whether you are giving feedback in a teacher session or receiving it.

rows: Giving feedback
Start with a genuine positive; give more positives than negatives; talk about the work, not the person; be specific and give an example.
Receiving feedback
Listen without defending; thank the person; choose one or two changes that would help most; then improve the work and rehearse again.

toolkit.title: Active listening guide
toolkit.intro: Active listening means attentively trying to understand a speaker, not just hearing their words while you wait to talk. Show it with these signals.

rows: Non-verbal feedback
Nodding, leaning forward, making eye contact.
Verbal feedback
Short signals such as 'I see', 'I understand', 'that makes sense'.
Check you understood
Say the speaker's key message back: 'So your main point is ...?'

toolkit.title: Visual and creative-outcome tips
toolkit.intro: A good visual or creative outcome makes your message faster to understand or easier to feel, not just prettier. Keep these in mind.
items: Use a chart when your evidence is numbers — it shows a pattern at a glance.
Keep posters simple: few words, large enough to read from a distance.
Add a slogan: short, clear, and memorable, giving a reason or a feeling.
Try a rap, song or poem to raise awareness and reach people a report never would.
Make sure every visual actually supports your key message, and remove anything that distracts.

toolkit.title: Register guide
toolkit.intro: Register is your level of formality. Match it to your audience.

rows: Young children
Simple, warm, friendly words; short sentences.
The beach is where the fish live, so we always take our rubbish home.
Family and community
Clear and friendly, still respectful.
Our coast is filling with plastic, and here is a simple way we can help.
Officials, such as a council
Formal, polite, evidence-first.
I respectfully ask the council to support reusable bags and regular clean-ups.

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for communicating
toolkit.intro: Use these to speak and write clearly. They work for talks, posters and written arguments.

toolkit.title: To introduce your piece
items: Today I will explain / show / argue that ...
This piece is about ...
My main message is that ...

toolkit.title: To give reasoning or introduce evidence
items: This matters because ...
For example, ... / For instance, ...
According to ... (source), ...
My survey / research found that ...

toolkit.title: To conclude with a personal perspective
items: To sum up, ...
Weighing all the evidence, I believe that ...
For all these reasons, my own view is that ...
As you can see, ...

toolkit.title: To listen actively and give feedback
items: I see. / I understand. / That makes sense.
So your main point is ...? (checking you understood)
One thing I really liked was ...
One idea to make it even better would be ...

checklists.title: Checklist: Before you present
checklists.intro: Tick each one. If you cannot tick them all, rehearse again.
items: Clear message — I can say my key message in one short sentence.
Structure — I have an introduction, a body and a conclusion with my personal perspective.
Argument — every paragraph has a claim, reasoning and evidence.
Reasoning — I use transition words like 'because' and 'for example'.
Sources — I can name where my evidence came from, and I cross-checked my key fact.
Voice — I will speak slowly and clearly, and pause after my message.
Register — my language and spelling suit my audience.
Fairness — I mention other perspectives honestly.
Rehearsed — I have practised the whole thing out loud at least twice.

challenge.intro:
You have now communicated a whole year's work. Pull it together by completing these three sentences about your Challenge, in your own words:

Keep this checkpoint safe. It is the final piece of your Year 8 journey, and it shows how much your communication has grown. Notice how much more confident you are now at turning a year of research, analysis and evaluation into one clear message for a real audience.
checkpoints: The clearest part of my message was ...
The part my audience understood least was ...
If I communicated this again, I would ...

activities.title: Decide your purpose and audience
activities.label: Activity 1: Decide your purpose and audience
activities.intro: Every strong piece of communication starts here. Before you plan anything, get clear on why you are communicating and who you are communicating with.
steps: Write your Challenge topic in one sentence: 'My Challenge is about ...'.
Name your purpose in one word: to inform, to persuade, or to raise awareness.
Describe your main audience (for example: my teacher session, my family, or the local community).
Write one sentence about what you want that audience to think, feel, or do by the end.

boxes.title: Malik's example: purpose and audience
lines: Topic: bringing solar power to our school at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa.
Purpose: to persuade, so the school tries one solar lamp in each classroom.
Audience: his teacher and the school's head teacher.
What he wants: for the school to test solar lamps and see the saving for itself.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your topic, your purpose and your audience.
Ask it: Does my purpose match my audience, or should I adjust one of them?
Ask the tutor how my chosen audience should change the way I speak or write.

activities.title: Write your key message
activities.label: Activity 2: Write your key message
activities.intro: Your key message is the one idea you most want your audience to remember. Everything else in your piece will support it, so it is worth getting right, and worth keeping short.
steps: Look back over your Challenge work from the year: your research, your analysis, your evaluation.
Ask yourself: if my audience forgot everything but one sentence, what should it be?
Write your key message as a single, short, clear sentence.
Read it aloud. If it takes more than one breath or needs a second sentence, trim it.

boxes.title: A model key message
lines: Weak: There are lots of things about the coast and plastic and the market and the fish near our town.
Strong: Reusable bags and monthly clean-ups can keep Berbera's coast clean.
The strong version is one short sentence an audience can hold in their head and repeat.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your key message to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Is this clear and focused, or is it trying to say too much at once?
Ask the tutor to suggest one shorter or sharper way to word my key message.

activities.title: Gather your evidence from the whole year
activities.label: Activity 3: Gather your evidence from the whole year
activities.intro:
This is the activity where your Challenge truly comes together. Communication does not invent facts; it arranges the ones you already earned. Go back through your Year 8 work and pull out your best material.

Aim for a mix: a number from a survey is convincing, but so is a short quotation from a person you interviewed, or a fact from a trusted report. If you can, cross-check your most important fact against a second source so you know it is reliable.
steps: From your Research: find two or three facts, numbers or quotations you can use as evidence.
From your Analysis: find one cause-and-effect idea that explains why your topic matters.
From your Evaluation: find your judgement about which solution or answer is strongest.
Next to each piece of evidence, note where it came from, so you can reference it later.

boxes.title: Leila's example: gathering evidence
lines: Leila's Challenge is about traffic near her school in Mogadishu.
From her research: 15 of 20 drivers she counted did not slow down at the corner.
From her analysis: fast traffic plus a blind corner is what makes it dangerous.
From her evaluation: she judged that a painted crossing was the cheapest useful fix.
She now has a number, a cause, and a judgement — ready to shape into paragraphs.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor the best evidence you have gathered and where each piece came from.
Ask it: Which piece is strongest, and which is weakest?
Ask the tutor how to mention the source of each piece of evidence when I present.

activities.title: Plan your structure - introduction, body, conclusion
activities.label: Activity 4: Plan your structure - introduction, body, conclusion
activities.intro: Now give your piece a clear shape. Use the three-part structure: an introduction linked to your research question, a body of several points with evidence, and a conclusion that sums up and gives your personal perspective without adding anything new.
steps: Introduction: write one or two sentences that say what your piece is about and state your key message.
Body: plan three points. For each, write the point in a few words. You will build them into full arguments next.
Conclusion: write one or two sentences that draw your points together and give your personal perspective. Add no new fact here.
Read the whole plan through. Does each part do its job?

boxes.title: A quick structure check
lines: Introduction: does it make clear what I am talking about and what I believe?
Body: does each point carry just one main idea?
Conclusion: does it sum up and give my personal view, with nothing new sneaking in?

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your introduction, three body points and conclusion to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the structure is clear and whether any point is doing two jobs at once.
Ask the tutor if my conclusion gives a personal perspective without adding a new fact.

activities.title: Build each paragraph into an argument and write your script
activities.label: Activity 5: Build each paragraph into an argument and write your script
activities.intro: Turn each body point into a full paragraph that is a small argument: a claim, reasoning, and evidence. Then write these paragraphs out as a script you can read aloud or record.
steps: For each body point, write the claim (what you want the audience to accept).
Add the reasoning (why the claim is true), often starting with the word 'because'.
Add the evidence (the fact, number or example that proves the reasoning) and name its source.
Write the three paragraphs, plus your introduction and conclusion, as one full script.

boxes.title: A model paragraph built as an argument
lines: Claim: Our market should switch to reusable cloth bags.
Reasoning: Because thin plastic bags block the drains and reach the sea.
Evidence: In my survey, most sellers agreed the drains flood in the rains.
Source: my own survey of 20 market sellers.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read one of your paragraphs to your AI tutor as a claim, reasoning and evidence.
Ask it: Does my reasoning really explain my claim, and does my evidence really prove my reasoning?
Ask the tutor to help me strengthen the weakest of my three paragraphs.

activities.title: Add transition words and check your paragraphing
activities.label: Activity 6: Add transition words and check your paragraphing
activities.intro: Now join your ideas so your audience can follow your thinking, and make sure each new paragraph starts in the right place.
steps: Read your script aloud. Where do the ideas feel jumpy or disconnected?
Add reasoning words such as 'because', 'therefore' and 'this means that'.
Add evidence words such as 'for example', 'for instance' and 'such as' before each fact.
Check that you start a new paragraph for each new point, and choose a phrase such as 'to sum up' or 'in conclusion' for your conclusion.

boxes.title: Handy transition words
lines: To give reasoning: because, so that, therefore, this means that, as a result.
To introduce evidence: for example, for instance, such as, to demonstrate.
To conclude: finally, in conclusion, to sum up, as you can see.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your linked-up script to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the transition words make your reasoning clearer, or whether any feel forced.
Ask the tutor whether each of my paragraphs really starts a new point.

activities.title: Design a visual or creative outcome
activities.label: Activity 7: Design a visual or creative outcome
activities.intro: Some of your audience will meet your message through a visual or a creative outcome rather than a talk. Design one now: a poster, a chart, a slogan, or a short rap, song or poem to carry your message quickly.
steps: Decide the clearest form for your message: a bar chart for numbers, a poster for awareness, or a short rap, song or poem to raise feeling.
Sketch or draft it. Keep it simple and easy to read or hear.
Write a slogan or a memorable line that captures your key message.
Test it: is it short, clear, and does it stick in the mind?

boxes.title: Model slogans and lines
lines: Plastic: Reuse your bag, protect our beach.
Water: Every drop counts — do not waste water.
Road safety: Slow down outside our school — keep students safe.
Notice each one is short, clear, and gives a reason or a feeling.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe your visual or creative outcome and read your slogan or line to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the form shows your message clearly and whether the line is memorable.
Ask the tutor for one way to make my slogan or line shorter or stronger.

activities.title: Match your language to your audience
activities.label: Activity 8: Match your language to your audience
activities.intro: Check that your register — your level of formality — fits your audience, and that your topic-specific words are correct. The same message should sound different for young children, for family, and for officials.
steps: Write your key message in a friendly register, as if speaking to a younger child or your family.
Write the same message in a formal register, as if writing to the town council or head teacher.
Decide which register fits the audience you chose in Activity 1.
Adjust your script so its language matches that audience throughout, and check your spelling.

boxes.title: Yasmin's example: one message, two registers
lines: Message: girls who leave school early lose chances that are hard to get back.
Friendly (for younger students): staying in school opens doors that are hard to open later.
Formal (for a community meeting): early school-leaving among girls reduces their future opportunities, and I ask you to consider how we might support them to stay.
Same message, matched to each audience.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your two versions — friendly and formal — to your AI tutor.
Ask it which register best fits my real audience, and why.
Ask the tutor to check that my script keeps that register from start to finish.

activities.title: Rehearse your full piece with your AI tutor
activities.label: Activity 9: Rehearse your full piece with your AI tutor
activities.intro: This is the most important activity in the unit. Before you present to real people, rehearse the whole thing out loud with your AI tutor acting as your audience. Rehearsing silently in your head is not the same; speaking out loud is what builds confidence.
steps: Present your whole piece out loud to your AI tutor, from introduction to conclusion.
Ask the tutor for feedback using the three fair rules: start positive, more positives than negatives, and about the work.
Improve the one weakest part it points out, then present again.
If you can, record your piece as a short podcast or voice note and listen back for anywhere you rushed.

boxes.title: Rehearsal tips
lines: Speak slowly and clearly, and pause after your key message.
Use a few bullet-point notes, not the full script read word for word.
Rehearse as many times as you like — your AI tutor never gets tired.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Present your full piece to your AI tutor and ask for honest feedback on clarity and pace.
Ask it to predict two questions a real audience might ask, and help me prepare answers.
Ask the tutor: what is the single most important thing to improve before my teacher session?

activities.title: Deliver, listen actively, and exchange feedback
activities.label: Activity 10: Deliver, listen actively, and exchange feedback
activities.intro:
Now for the real thing. You have rehearsed; you are ready. Deliver your piece in your teacher session, and when it is someone else's turn, listen actively and give and receive feedback.

It is completely normal to feel nervous, even after rehearsing. Nerves are a sign that you care, not a sign that you are unprepared. Take a slow breath, remember you know your topic better than anyone in the room, and keep your key message in mind. Because you practised out loud with your AI tutor, your voice already knows the way.
steps: Deliver your piece to your teacher and the other learners. Speak slowly, and remember your key message.
When others present, listen actively: nod, make eye contact, and use signals like 'I see'.
Give one classmate feedback using the three fair rules, and thank anyone who gives feedback to you.
Note down the questions your own audience asked, and one change you will make as a result.

boxes.title: Share it at home and in your community
lines: Present your Challenge to a family member or neighbour, in a register that suits them.
Ask them what they think should be done about your topic, and listen to their answer.
Bring their response, and any questions they asked, to your next teacher session.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor how your real delivery went and what questions or feedback you received.
Ask it to help me understand what those questions show about the clearest and weakest parts of my piece.
Ask the tutor to help me plan one improvement for the next time I communicate.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Try every question before you look at the answer key, and give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'communication' mean?
practice.answer: Communication means transferring information from one person to another, by speaking or writing, so that the other person truly understands. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: Communication has two halves: expressing your own ideas and ______ to others.
practice.answer: Listening.

practice.prompt: Before you plan any piece, you should know two things: your purpose and your ______.
practice.answer: Audience.

practice.prompt: Name the three main parts of a well-structured piece.
practice.answer: Introduction, body (or middle), and conclusion.

practice.prompt: In Stage 8, a conclusion should sum up the points and also give your ______ perspective.
practice.answer: Personal.

practice.prompt: A well-structured paragraph is built from three parts: a claim, reasoning, and ______.
practice.answer: Evidence.

practice.prompt: True or false: a good conclusion is the perfect place to add an exciting new fact.
practice.answer: False. A conclusion sums up what you already said and gives your personal perspective; it should not add new ideas.

practice.prompt: Give one transition word or phrase you could use to introduce a piece of evidence.
practice.answer: Any one of: for example, for instance, such as, to demonstrate.

practice.prompt: When you present out loud, should you speak quickly to save time, or slowly and clearly?
practice.answer: Slowly and clearly.

practice.prompt: Name one creative outcome (other than a talk) you could use to raise awareness.
practice.answer: Any one of: a poster, a chart, a slogan, a rap, a song, a poem, a short video or podcast.

practice.prompt: The word ______ means the level of formality in your language, chosen to suit your audience.
practice.answer: Register.

practice.prompt: Active listening means attentively trying to ______ someone, not just hearing their words.
practice.answer: Understand (attentively trying to understand the person).

practice.prompt: Name one of the three fair rules for giving feedback on someone's work.
practice.answer: Any one of: start with a positive; give more positives than negatives; talk about the work, not the person; be specific and give an example.

practice.prompt: Checking that a fact appears on more than one trustworthy source is called ______.
practice.answer: Cross-referencing.

practice.prompt: Give one reason why you should reference the sources of your evidence when you communicate.
practice.answer: Any one of: it is honest and avoids copying; it lets the audience check your facts; it makes your work more trustworthy.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each communication word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Register
options: A. Attentively trying to understand what someone says, not just hearing the words.
B. A claim supported by reasoning and evidence.
C. Choosing your level of formality to suit your audience and purpose.
D. Checking a fact against more than one trustworthy source.
E. The part of a piece that sums up the points and gives your own view, adding nothing new.
F. What you personally think about an issue after weighing the evidence.
practice.answer: C — Choosing your level of formality to suit your audience and purpose.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Argument
practice.answer: B — A claim supported by reasoning and evidence.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Personal perspective
practice.answer: F — What you personally think about an issue after weighing the evidence.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Active listening
practice.answer: A — Attentively trying to understand what someone says, not just hearing the words.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Cross-referencing
practice.answer: D — Checking a fact against more than one trustworthy source.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Conclusion
practice.answer: E — The part of a piece that sums up the points and gives your own view, adding nothing new.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Nadia is presenting about hand-washing to a class of six-year-olds. Should her register be formal and technical, or simple and friendly? Why?
practice.answer: Simple and friendly. Six-year-olds would not follow formal, technical language, so a warm, simple register suits them best.

practice.prompt: Omar ends his talk by suddenly adding a brand-new statistic he never mentioned before. Which rule of a good conclusion has he broken?
practice.answer: He added a new idea in the conclusion. A conclusion should only sum up points already made and give a personal perspective, not introduce new facts.

practice.prompt: Talia writes 'our school meals are unhealthy' but gives nothing else. What one thing should she add so the audience believes her?
practice.answer: Evidence. She should add a fact, number or example (and its source) so the audience has a reason to believe her.

practice.prompt: During Imani's talk, Grace nods and quietly says 'I see.' What is she doing, and why does it help?
practice.answer: She is listening actively and giving verbal and non-verbal feedback. It helps because it shows Imani she is paying attention and understanding her.

practice.prompt: Rohan finds a striking fact on a personal blog. What should he do before he uses it as evidence, and why?
practice.answer: He should cross-check it against a second, more trustworthy source, because a personal blog usually gives an opinion rather than checked facts.

Rehearsing and talking with my AI tutor ...
Presenting, discussing and exchanging feedback in my teacher sessions ...
Sharing my Challenge with family or neighbours ...

vocabulary.meaning: Transferring information from one person to another, usually by speaking or writing.
The reason you are communicating: to inform, to persuade, or to raise awareness.
The people you are communicating with.
The single most important idea you want your audience to remember.
How a piece is organised so the audience can follow it easily.
The opening that links to the title or question and states the message.
The middle of a piece, made of paragraphs that give the points and evidence.
The ending that sums up the points and gives a personal perspective, adding nothing new.
A group of sentences presenting one point, its reasoning and its evidence.
A claim supported by reasoning and evidence.
A statement or assertion that something is true.
The justification for a claim, often introduced by 'because'.
A fact, number or example that supports a claim.
A place from which information or evidence is obtained.
A note saying exactly where information came from.
All the sources used, gathered together at the end of a piece.
Checking that a detail is the same on more than one source.
Linking words that connect ideas, such as because, therefore and for example.
What you personally think about an issue after weighing the evidence.
A particular point of view on an issue.
The level of formality in language, chosen to suit the audience.
A short, memorable phrase used to raise awareness of an issue.
A product, such as a poster, talk or poem, made to achieve a purpose.
Attentively trying to understand a speaker, not just hearing their words.
Spoken signals that show you are listening, such as 'I see' or 'I understand'.
Signals without words, such as nodding, leaning forward, or eye contact.
Helpful information given to someone about their work.
Words that are closely related to your topic.
When a source or speaker leans unfairly to one side.

mistakes: Starting to plan before you know your purpose and audience.
Having no clear key message, so the audience misses your point.
Making a claim with no reasoning or evidence behind it.
Sneaking a brand-new idea into the conclusion instead of giving your perspective.
Speaking too fast and never pausing.
Using a register that does not fit the audience.
Forgetting to reference or cross-check where your evidence came from.
Only speaking, and never really listening or acting on feedback.

selfAssessment.statement: I can plan a piece of communication for a clear purpose and audience.
I can say my key message in one short, clear sentence.
I can organise my ideas into an introduction, a body and a conclusion.
I can build a paragraph as a claim with reasoning and evidence.
I can reference and cross-check the sources my evidence came from.
I can use transition words to give reasoning and connect my ideas.
I can present clearly out loud, speaking slowly and with detail.
I can present my ideas visually or creatively, for example with a poster or a slogan.
I can choose suitable language and register for my audience.
